catalog_quote: Primary stress in Old Rapa is directly related to the relative weight of syllables, where surface long vowels and surface diphthongs (both long and short) attract stress as a result of their heavier weight. Thus, stress in Old Rapa is predictable based on the metrical structure of the base. In Old Rapa, the prosodic foot consists of two or three mora and is built from the right edge of the word. Primary stress falls regularly on the penultimate mora (3.43). ... In words with more than one foot, primary stress falls on the penultimate mora of the second (counting from the right) foot. ... a foot consists of either one heavy syllable or two light syllables. In Old Rapa, a heavy syllable attracts stress; therefore, a foot with a heavy syllable will take stress. ... audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The record rests on Walworth 2015, a 316-pp modern descriptive grammar (PhD dissertation) that Glottolog lists as the sole grammar of the language; we hold the PDF and every deciding quotation (primary stress pp. 61-65, preview p. 43, domain p. 61, secondary stress pp. 65-66) is present verbatim at the stated locators. The source explicitly states a right-edge moraic-foot system in which heavy (CVV: long vowel > diphthong) syllables attract stress, matching classification weight, edge=right, what counts as heavy: CVV. Searches of Crossref, HAL, MPG PuRe and UH ScholarSpace surfaced no phonology article, instrumental study or JIPA illustration for Rapa; the two open items downloaded now (Charpentier & Francois 2015 atlas; Walworth 2017 'Classifying Old Rapa', scanned) are silent on stress.
